newsitem.title: USA: Defense rests its case in Simpson civil trial.
newsitem.headline: Defense rests its case in Simpson civil trial.

text.p: The defence in O.J. Simpson's civil trial rested its case on Tuesday and the plaintiffs began calling rebuttal witnesses, including a photographer who took shots of Simpson wearing Bruno Magli shoes.

FBI shoeprint expert William Bodziak testified earlier that the Italian designer shoes left the trail of bloody prints leading from the scene where Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman were stabbed to death on June 12, 1994.

Simpson, who was acquitted in October 1995 of the murders of his ex-wife and her friend and now faces a wrongful-death civil suit brought by the victims' families, has denied ever owning a pair of Bruno Maglis.

Testifying as the plaintiffs' first rebuttal witness, E.J. Flammer, a 24-year-old freelance photographer, told the jury he was at Rich Stadium in Buffalo for the Sept. 26, 1993, Buffalo Bills football game.
He said that before the game he took 30 photos of Simpson with a group of five men, who were planning a 20-year anniversary celebration of Simpson's first 2,000-yard rushing season.

Flammer said he made six colour photographs for the men and one black and white photograph for the Buffalo Bills Report, a fan newsletter. The negatives remained in his darkroom until Dec. 27, 1996, when he hired an agent and a lawyer, he added.

The last witness in the defence portion of the case was the ex-football star's eldest daughter, Arnelle, who testified that her father was "shocked, very upset, sad, confused" when he learned of his ex-wife's death by telephone in his Chicago hotel room.
Taking the stand the day after her father finished testifying, Arnelle Simpson, 28, told jurors how she was awakened by two detectives at about 5.30 a.m. on the day after the murders.
"They asked me where my father was and I said I didn't know where he was but I knew somebody who could get in touch with him," she said.
She said she took the detectives to the main section of her father's mansion and then went to her car to get the telephone number of Simpson's personal secretary.

"When I was going out to the car I asked them 'Please tell me what's going on, please tell me what's happened. At that point (Det. Philip Vannatter) said that Nicole ... had been killed at her house and that there was someone else with her," Arnelle Simpson said.
Asked how she reacted to the news she she replied, "I was shocked, I was stunned, upset, confused and scared."

She said she spoke to her father, who was in Chicago, where he had flown late the previous night. "He kept saying 'What's going on, what's going on?' and all I could tell him was Nicole's dead and there's somebody else with her," Arnelle Simpson said.
"He was shocked, very upset, sad, confused," she added.
After Arnelle Simpson left the witness stand, she sat behind her father, who turned around, clenched her hand and smiled at her.

The defence started its case on Dec. 9 last year but because of a two-week Christmas and New Year holiday break and other days when the court was not in session, testimony from defence witnesses took only 14 working days to complete. This was in sharp contrast to the defence in Simpson's criminal trial, which was presented over a period of four months.
The rebuttal phase will be followed by closing arguments, which could begin by Friday or early next week. The jury is expected to get the case for deliberation by the end of January.
If Simpson is found responsible for the murders, he faces no threat of jail time but could be forced to pay millions of dollars in damages.
